# Introduction to the Second Half {#sec-intro-advanced .unnumbered}

In this introduction we shall describe what the second half of
the book contains and what we mean by calling it advanced. We
then set out the two commitments that the subtitle places on
every chapter, the dependencies that govern reading order, and
the topics we have chosen to leave aside.

## What the second half is

The first half of this book covers programming, numerical
linear algebra, optimization, simulation, the bootstrap, the
standard frequentist models, and statistical graphics. It is
written for the first quarter of a two-quarter graduate
sequence. The second half begins here, where the first leaves
off, and is written for the second quarter. In print it is
Volume II.

## What 'advanced' means here

The word 'advanced' carries three meanings in the second half,
which we take in increasing strength.

The first is a deeper treatment of foundational topics.
@sec-numerical-stability and @sec-numerical-linalg, on
numerical stability and numerical linear algebra, revisit
material that the first half touches but does not treat in
depth. Floating-point arithmetic, condition numbers, sparse and
iterative solvers, and BLAS-level performance are fundamentals.
Everything after them depends on them.

The second is topics that exceed introductory scope.
@sec-advanced-optimization through @sec-modern-bayesian take
up advanced optimization, the EM algorithm and its extensions,
Monte Carlo in depth, Bayesian computation, MCMC in depth, and
modern Bayesian computation. Each chapter extends the
first-half treatment of its topic. The aim is to reach the
territory needed for current methodological research and for
applied practice with modern tools.

The third is topics that did not appear in the first half at
all. @sec-parallel through @sec-interactive-viz take up
parallel and high-performance computing, high-dimensional
methods, machine learning, R package development and testing,
software engineering for statisticians, reproducible
computational environments, and interactive applications and
dashboards. The first half deliberately sets this ground aside.
Each of these is the kind of topic a practicing biostatistician
meets mid-career, and graduate training ought to prepare the
reader for it.

## What 'in the Age of AI' commits the second half to

The subtitle commits every chapter to two named sections.

The first, **The statistician's contribution**, is placed
early. It states explicitly the judgments at the center of the
chapter that no large language model can make on the reader's
behalf. Advanced material is exactly where the
division of labor between human and LLM matters most. To
illustrate, a careless prompt in an introductory bootstrap
chapter produces a bug that a rerun will catch. A careless
prompt in a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo or a high-dimensional
chapter produces results that look plausible and are wrong.
The stakes rise further when the prompt is handed to a coding
agent rather than typed into a chat window, since the agent
edits the analysis code and reruns the pipeline unattended. In
that case nothing forces a human to see the intermediate step
where the mistake was made.

The second, **Collaborating with an LLM on the topic at
hand**, comes at the end of the chapter. It offers specific
prompts, each paired with what to watch for and how to verify
the result. That is, each prompt is structured as a triple:
the prompt itself, the failure modes the model may exhibit,
and a verification step the reader runs to catch them. We
apply the framework uniformly across the second half, as in
the first.

## Reading order

The chapters may be read in order or out of order, subject to
the following dependencies.

- @sec-numerical-stability and @sec-numerical-linalg, the
  numerical foundations, underpin all the numerical work in
  @sec-advanced-optimization through @sec-modern-bayesian.
- @sec-advanced-optimization feeds @sec-em-extensions, the EM
  algorithm and its extensions, and @sec-high-dim,
  high-dimensional methods.
- @sec-monte-carlo, Monte Carlo, feeds @sec-bayesian, Bayesian
  computation, which feeds @sec-mcmc-depth, MCMC, which in
  turn feeds @sec-modern-bayesian, modern Bayesian
  computation.
- @sec-parallel, parallel computing, comes before @sec-hpc,
  high-performance and distributed computing.
- @sec-packages, package development, comes before
  @sec-testing, testing, and both come before
  @sec-software-engineering and
  @sec-reproducible-environments.
- @sec-shiny, Shiny, comes before @sec-interactive-viz,
  interactive visualization and dashboards.
- Otherwise the computing and software chapters are largely
  independent of one another and of the numerical chapters,
  with one exception: @sec-machine-learning uses the
  optimization tools of @sec-advanced-optimization.

A reader who follows the dependencies in order will treat the
second half as a course. A reader who picks topics as needed
will treat it as a reference.

## What this book does not cover

We have set aside several topics that are usually taught in
dedicated methods courses elsewhere in a biostatistics
curriculum:

- Causal inference computing.
- Longitudinal data analysis beyond the introductory GLMM
  material.
- Missing-data computing in depth.
- Meta-analysis.

We point the reader to the standard references for each as
they arise.

## Software environment

The second half assumes a current R installation, a current
Quarto, and the package set used in the first half. We name
new software in the chapter that uses it. The companion
*Biostatistics Practicum* documents the workflow, the
infrastructure, and the deployment conventions that we assume
throughout.
